speaker: Zoltan Pozsar
title: Zoltan Pozsar on His Next Big Move and the Coming Monetary Divorce
question: In commercial banking, what balance-sheet dynamics turn a sector downturn and rising rates into an acute run on a specialized bank?
guest: SVB is a case where, on the liability side, if you think about the tech and venture capital sector where valuations took a big nosedive after tech stocks corrected, you had a depositor base that was liquidity constrained, so they pulled money from one bank where a lot of tech entrepreneurs kept their cash. That's a liquidity drain, and the deposit base wasn't diversified. On the asset side, SVB had a lot of duration. Going through the call reports of the biggest institutions, very few banks had as big a share of their rate-related portfolio in stripped mortgage-backed securities as they did. They had a lot of coupon exposure, a lot of principal exposure, and a lot of duration in these portfolios, and they didn't hedge them properly. They also had a lending book where they were lending to the same customers who were pulling funds away from them, with tech-related collateral facing valuation issues.

points.core: An undiversified depositor base facing a shared downturn drains bank liquidity simultaneously.
points.note: Accept: concentrated single-sector depositors (e.g., tech/VC startups) becoming liquidity-constrained at once and withdrawing cash together. Do not credit: generic statements about social media panic or uninsured deposits alone.

points.core: Unhedged duration exposure in long-dated securities inflicts severe interest-rate asset losses.
points.note: Accept: holding long-duration bonds or stripped MBS without interest-rate hedges causing deep valuation losses when rates rise. Do not credit: vague mentions of bad investments or credit defaults on Treasuries.

points.core: Lending to the same sector erodes loan collateral alongside deposit outflows.
points.note: Accept: wrong-way risk where borrowers are the same struggling depositors and loan collateral values drop simultaneously. Do not credit: generic warnings to diversify a bank's business.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
A specialized bank is exposed on both sides of its balance sheet to the same shock, and the two sides reinforce each other.

On the liability side, its deposits come from a concentrated group of clients in one sector, often in large, uninsured balances. When that sector turns down, those clients burn cash and draw down deposits simultaneously, so funding shrinks just as a diversified bank's would not.

On the asset side, the bank typically invested its earlier deposit inflows in long-duration, fixed-rate securities and loans. Rising rates cut their market value, creating large unrealized losses, often hidden by held-to-maturity accounting. Rising rates also raise the cost of retaining deposits while asset yields stay locked in, squeezing margins.

The trigger comes when outflows force the bank to sell securities, turning paper losses into realized ones that dent capital. A loss announcement or capital raise then signals weakness. Uninsured depositors, who are tightly networked and able to move money instantly, have every incentive to leave first, and the run becomes self-fulfilling: more withdrawals force more fire sales, converting a liquidity problem into insolvency. Silicon Valley Bank in 2023 is the canonical case.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer: A specialized bank becomes fragile when concentrated, uninsured liabilities collide with duration-mismatched assets. Normally, sticky core deposits hedge rising rates by providing cheap, stable funding even as fixed-rate asset values fall. In a specialized bank, however, clients clustered in one industry suffer correlated cash burn and dwindling inflows during a downturn, while higher rates pull remaining commercial balances into money market funds, breaking that deposit hedge. Simultaneously on the asset side, rising rates depress the market value of long-duration securities and loans while the downturn weakens sector credit quality and collateral values, creating deep unrealized losses that erode economic equity even when held-to-maturity accounting shields regulatory capital. Once persistent withdrawals exhaust cash buffers and borrowing capacity, the bank must sell underwater available-for-sale securities—or risk tainting its held-to-maturity portfolio—crystallizing hidden losses into a visible capital deficit. Recognizing that mark-to-market insolvency and shrinking liquidity cannot repay everyone at par, large, networked uninsured depositors race to withdraw first, turning gradual attrition into an acute run.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer: The core problem is a mismatch on both sides of the balance sheet that turns into a self-reinforcing loop. On the liability side, a specialized bank (SVB with tech and venture firms, Signature and Silvergate with crypto) draws deposits from one concentrated, connected client base, and most of those deposits are above the insurance limit, so depositors have every reason to flee early. When their sector slows, those clients burn cash and pull deposits all at once. On the asset side, the bank put its deposit surge into long-duration fixed-rate securities, often held-to-maturity, which hid unrealized losses as rates rose. Rate hikes cut the market value of those assets just as deposits drain. To meet withdrawals, the bank has to sell securities, which turns paper losses into real losses and eats into capital. That forces a public capital raise, which tells depositors there's a problem. Because they're networked and can move money instantly online, withdrawals snowball within hours, as at SVB, where $42 billion left in one day. Thin liquid buffers, weak interest-rate hedging, and slow access to backstop funding make it worse.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer: A specialized bank typically funds itself with large, uninsured deposits concentrated in a single industry, while investing surplus cash into long-duration, fixed-rate assets such as government or mortgage-backed securities. When interest rates rise sharply, the market value of those long-dated assets falls, creating substantial unrealized losses that erode the bank's economic equity even if accounting rules shield regulatory capital while the securities remain held to maturity. Simultaneously, a downturn in the bank's core sector reduces client inflows and accelerates cash burn, driving correlated deposit withdrawals. Once liquid reserves are exhausted, the bank must sell underwater securities to meet outflows, converting paper losses into realized capital hits—or attempt an emergency equity raise that signals distress. Because uninsured depositors have a strong incentive to exit before losses impair solvency, visible capital strain triggers a self-fulfilling panic, turning steady liquidity pressure into an acute run.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
A specialized bank can have both borrowers and depositors exposed to the same industry. When that industry slumps, customers draw down deposits to cover expenses, and some borrowers struggle to repay. If deposits are concentrated among businesses with large uninsured balances, many customers can pull substantial sums at once.

Rising rates meanwhile reduce the market value of the bank’s long-term, fixed-rate assets. The bank owes depositors their full balances on demand, but it may have to sell assets at a loss to raise cash. Those sales can turn unrealized losses into losses that erode reported capital just as weakening loans threaten further losses. If depositors see asset sales or an emergency capital raise as signs the bank may struggle to pay, they have an incentive to withdraw before others do. The run becomes acute when withdrawals outpace the bank’s ability to raise cash through borrowing or asset sales.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
A specialized bank may lend to and take deposits from the same industry. When that sector turns down, borrowers become riskier just as customers draw down deposits to cover expenses. If many deposits exceed insurance limits, a large share of the bank’s funding can leave as soon as customers fear losses.

Rising rates intensify the squeeze. Depositors can earn more elsewhere, replacement funding costs more, and the market value of long-term fixed-rate loans and securities falls. The bank may be able to hold those assets to maturity, but it owes depositors cash on demand. Once withdrawals exceed available cash and borrowing capacity, it may have to sell assets at a loss, eroding capital. A disclosed loss or an urgent capital raise can prompt closely connected depositors to withdraw together. That feedback loop turns a funding squeeze into an acute run, even before widespread loan defaults occur.
